claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance in multiprincipal-element alloys is governed by the rapid formation of a continuous protective oxide scale.
Maintenance of material integrity is governed by formation of an adherent protective oxide scale.
Cr and Al are protective oxide-forming elements in high-temperature alloys.
Superior oxidation resistance can result from synergy between alloy chemistry and a nanocrystalline microstructure.
Grain refinement produces a high density of grain boundaries that act as short-circuit diffusion paths for Al and Cr.
Accelerated transport of Al and Cr to the surface promotes formation of a continuous protective scale.
A protective oxide scale limits further oxygen ingress and thereby lowers oxidation.
The protective scale prevents depletion of bulk alloying elements needed to maintain mechanical integrity.
Nanocrystalline alloys will form more uniform oxide scales than coarse-grained baseline alloys.
Nanocrystalline alloys will form more adherent oxide scales than coarse-grained baseline alloys.
Nanocrystalline or compositionally optimized alloys will show lower oxidation rates, measurable as reduced mass gain.
Nanocrystalline or compositionally optimized alloys will retain mechanical properties better after oxidation than the baseline.
A coarse-grained alloy with lower effective concentrations of protective elements will form discontinuous, less adherent scales and oxidize faster.
The proposed mechanism holds in air over approximately 800–1200 °C.
The mechanism may not apply well outside 800–1200 °C or in non-oxidizing environments.
The relative contributions of protective-element concentration and grain-boundary diffusion-path density vary with alloy system and temperature.
A same-composition nanocrystalline-versus-coarse-grained comparison at about 1000 °C can test the effect of microstructural refinement.
Failure of the refined, optimized alloy to show statistically significant improvements in scale quality, mass gain, and mechanical-property retention would falsify the proposed synergy.

contradictions.description: The experiment initially requires identical bulk compositions, but then permits alloying adjustment and describes the control as having lower effective protective-element levels. This confounds microstructure with chemistry and contradicts the stated same-composition comparison.

The hypothesis proposes a synergy between chemistry and microstructure, whereas the falsification rule treats failure to improve all three outcomes as falsifying the synergy without separately testing either factor or their interaction.
